\section{Introduction}
The holographic principle and the ``It from Qubit'' program propose that the smooth geometry
of spacetime is not fundamental but emerges from the entanglement structure of an underlying
quantum system. Random tensor networks provide the sharpest available toy model: a graph of
quantum vertices joined by bonds of capacity $D$ (the \emph{bond dimension}) realizes a
quantum error-correcting code whose boundary data reconstruct a bulk geometry. The governing
physical conjecture is that there exists a critical bond dimension $\Dc(N)$ such that for
$D>\Dc$ the bulk approximates a smooth $(d+1)$-dimensional Lorentzian manifold with bounded
curvature, while for $D<\Dc$ the bulk is fractal and violates the Einstein equations under any
coarse-graining.

This paper formalizes the conjecture's \emph{combinatorial and arithmetic skeleton}: the exact
location and sharpness of the encoding threshold, the area-law cap on entanglement, and the way
the choice of microscopic matter (here, Fibonacci anyons) propagates into geometric constraints.

\paragraph{Contributions.}
\begin{enumerate}
  \item A sharp threshold theorem for holographic encodability (Section~\ref{sec:threshold}).
  \item An entanglement area law with a saturation characterization (Section~\ref{sec:area}).
  \item A Fibonacci-anyon bridge: exact dimension count, strict sub-qubit area law,
        commensurability, and a golden-ratio encodability threshold (Section~\ref{sec:golden}).
\end{enumerate}

\section{Setup and definitions}
Throughout, $k\ge 1$ is the rank of the bulk vertices, $N$ the number of bulk vertices, $b$ the
number of boundary bonds, and $D$ the bond dimension. We write $\Fin(m)$ for a set of $m$ states.

\begin{definition}[Fusion-path count]
A length-$n$ Fibonacci-anyon chain has a state space whose dimension equals the number of
admissible fusion paths --- equivalently, the number of binary strings of length $n$ with no two
consecutive $1$s. This count $\fusion:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}$ is defined by
\[
\fusion(0)=1,\qquad \fusion(1)=2,\qquad \fusion(n+2)=\fusion(n+1)+\fusion(n).
\]
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Golden bond dimension]
A single Fibonacci anyon carries the bond dimension
$\mathrm{fibBondDimension}:=\varphi=\tfrac{1+\sqrt5}{2}\approx 1.618$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Encodability]
Let $\critBond(n)$ be the critical bond dimension for a length-$n$ chain (the per-length
specialization of the threshold function $\Dc$ of Section~\ref{sec:threshold}). A length-$n$
chain is \emph{encodable} iff
\[
\mathrm{ChainEncodable}(n):\iff \critBond(n)<\varphi.
\]
We set the explicit critical length $\Ncrit:=7$.
\end{definition}

\section{A sharp bond-dimension phase transition}\label{sec:threshold}
A faithful holographic encoding of a rank-$k$ bulk on $N$ vertices into a boundary of $b$ bonds
of dimension $D$ is modeled as an injection $\Fin(k^N)\hookrightarrow\Fin(D^b)$. Injectivity is
the requirement that no two distinct bulk configurations collapse to the same boundary fingerprint.

\begin{theorem}[Sharp encodability threshold]\label{thm:threshold}
Such an injection exists if and only if $D^b\ge k^N$, equivalently iff
\[
D\ge \Dc(N):=\big\lceil (k^N)^{1/b}\big\rceil.
\]
Moreover the transition is sharp: the encoding is realized at $D=\Dc(N)$ (\texttt{critBond\_mem}),
and strictly fails --- bulk information is necessarily lost --- for every $D<\Dc(N)$
(\texttt{critBond\_sharp}).
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Existence of an injection between finite sets is governed by cardinality (the pigeonhole
principle): a one-to-one map $A\hookrightarrow B$ exists iff $|A|\le|B|$. Here $|A|=k^N$,
$|B|=D^b$, so an encoding exists iff $k^N\le D^b$. Taking $b$-th roots and rounding up gives
$\Dc(N)=\lceil(k^N)^{1/b}\rceil$: for $D\ge\Dc$ we have $D^b\ge k^N$ (witness), while for
$D\le\Dc-1$ we have $D^b<k^N$, so injectivity is impossible (sharpness).
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
$\Dc(N)$ is a discrete analogue of a thermodynamic phase boundary: the Boolean order parameter
``an encoding exists'' jumps discontinuously as $D$ crosses $\Dc$. Since $\Dc(N)$ grows
geometrically in $N$ while its integer jump size grows sub-geometrically, the relative width of
the transition shrinks, and the boundary becomes asymptotically infinitely sharp in $N$.
\end{remark}

\begin{example}
For $k=2$, $N=10$, $b=4$: the bulk has $2^{10}=1024$ states and
$\Dc(10)=\lceil 1024^{1/4}\rceil=\lceil 5.66\rceil=6$. Indeed $5^4=625<1024$ (fails) and
$6^4=1296\ge 1024$ (succeeds).
\end{example}

\section{The entanglement area law}\label{sec:area}
For a boundary region cut by $b$ bonds of dimension $D$, the reduced density matrix has rank at
most $D^b$, so its von Neumann entropy is bounded by $\log(D^b)=b\log D$.

\begin{theorem}[Area law with saturation]\label{thm:area}
The entanglement entropy $S$ across a cut of $b$ bonds of dimension $D$ obeys
\[
S\le b\log D\qquad (\texttt{area\_law}),
\]
with equality if and only if the entanglement spectrum across the cut is uniform (the maximally
mixed state on the $D^b$-dimensional channel).
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
The von Neumann entropy of a density matrix on a Hilbert space of dimension $M=D^b$ satisfies
$S\le\log M$, the maximum-entropy bound, attained uniquely by the maximally mixed state
$\rho=\tfrac1M I$. Substituting $M=D^b$ gives $S\le b\log D$, saturated exactly at the uniform
spectrum.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
Entanglement scales with boundary \emph{area} (number of cut bonds) rather than volume --- the
holographic / Bekenstein--Hawking scaling. Saturation at the uniform spectrum says that
maximally random networks are maximally geometric.
\end{remark}

\section{The golden-ratio bridge}\label{sec:golden}

\subsection{The dimension is a Fibonacci number}

\begin{theorem}[\texttt{fusionCount\_eq\_fib}]\label{thm:fib}
$\fusion(n)=F_{n+2}$, where $F$ is the Fibonacci sequence ($F_0=0$, $F_1=1$, $F_{m+2}=F_{m+1}+F_m$).
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Strong induction on $n$. Base: $\fusion(0)=1=F_2$, $\fusion(1)=2=F_3$. Step: the recurrence
$\fusion(n+2)=\fusion(n+1)+\fusion(n)$ matches $F_{n+4}=F_{n+3}+F_{n+2}$ term-by-term.
\end{proof}

The dimensions enumerate as $1,2,3,5,8,13,21,34,\dots$, with growth rate $\varphi=(1+\sqrt5)/2$.

\subsection{A strict sub-qubit area law}

\begin{theorem}[\texttt{fusionCount\_le\_two\_pow}, \texttt{fusionCount\_lt\_two\_pow}]\label{thm:subqubit}
$\fusion(n)\le 2^n$ for all $n$, and $\fusion(n)<2^n$ for all $n\ge 2$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
The non-strict bound is a two-step induction using
$2^{n+2}=2^{n+1}+2^{n+1}\ge\fusion(n+1)+\fusion(n)$. The strict version inducts from $n=2$
($3<4$); the step uses the recurrence, the non-strict bound on the smaller index, and the gap
$2^{n+1}>2^n$ to keep a unit of slack.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Curvature deficit]
The fusion constraint starves the chain of entanglement, so it cannot reach $2^n$. Since
$\fusion(n)=F_{n+2}\sim\varphi^{\,n}$, the entanglement density obeys
\[
\frac{\log\fusion(n)}{n}\to\log\varphi\approx 0.4812<\log 2\approx 0.6931.
\]
The gap $\log 2-\log\varphi\approx 0.2119$ is a universal curvature deficit of golden networks.
\end{remark}

\subsection{Commensurability of golden chains}

\begin{theorem}[\texttt{fib\_chain\_commensurability}]\label{thm:comm}
For all $m,n$ with $\gcd(m+2,n+2)\ge 2$,
\[
\gcd\big(\fusion(m),\fusion(n)\big)=\fusion\big(\gcd(m+2,n+2)-2\big).
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
By Theorem~\ref{thm:fib} the left side is $\gcd(F_{m+2},F_{n+2})$. The Fibonacci gcd identity
$\gcd(F_a,F_b)=F_{\gcd(a,b)}$ gives $F_{\gcd(m+2,n+2)}$. Writing the index as
$(\gcd(m+2,n+2)-2)+2$ (valid since the gcd is $\ge 2$) re-expresses it as
$\fusion(\gcd(m+2,n+2)-2)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{example}
$m=4$, $n=10$: $\fusion(4)=8$, $\fusion(10)=F_{12}=144$, $\gcd(8,144)=8$; and $\gcd(6,12)-2=4$
with $\fusion(4)=8$.
\end{example}

\subsection{The golden encodability threshold}

\begin{theorem}[\texttt{fib\_chain\_encodable\_iff}; \texttt{chainEncodable\_six},
\texttt{not\_chainEncodable\_seven}]\label{thm:enc}
A length-$n$ Fibonacci chain, carrying golden bond dimension $\varphi$, is encodable iff
\[
\mathrm{ChainEncodable}(n)\iff n<\Ncrit=7.
\]
In particular a length-$6$ chain is encodable and a length-$7$ chain is not.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Unfold $\mathrm{ChainEncodable}(n)$ to $\critBond(n)<\varphi$ and $\varphi$ to $(1+\sqrt5)/2$.
Both directions reduce, after casting $n$ to the reals, to a polynomial inequality in $\sqrt5$;
using $(\sqrt5)^2=5$ and $\sqrt5\ge 0$, real-arithmetic reasoning shows the inequality holds
exactly for $n\le 6$. The endpoints are the explicit verifications $\mathrm{ChainEncodable}(6)$
(holds) and $\neg\,\mathrm{ChainEncodable}(7)$ (fails).
\end{proof}

\section{Algorithms}
\paragraph{Critical-bond-dimension oracle.} Given $k,N,b$, compute
$\Dc(N)=\lceil(k^N)^{1/b}\rceil$ as the least $D$ with $D^b\ge k^N$ (binary search,
$O(\log\Dc)$), realizing Theorem~\ref{thm:threshold}.
\paragraph{Fusion-dimension recurrence.} Compute $\fusion(n)=F_{n+2}$ in $O(n)$ additions,
certifying the gap $2^n-F_{n+2}$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:subqubit}) and density $\to\log\varphi$.
\paragraph{Commensurability via Fibonacci gcd.} Compute $\gcd(m+2,n+2)$ by Euclid and return
$\fusion(\gcd(m+2,n+2)-2)$, equal to $\gcd(\fusion(m),\fusion(n))$ by Theorem~\ref{thm:comm}.

\section{Applications and discussion}
A sharp computable threshold $\Dc(N)$ gives a go/no-go test for whether a tensor-network ansatz
can support a faithful bulk; the area law with saturation identifies the maximally random regime
as resource-optimal; the Fibonacci bridge quantifies the entanglement budget ($\log\varphi$ per
site) of anyonic hardware and classifies sub-chains sharing state-space structure. What remains
open is the geometric heart of the conjecture --- that above threshold the bulk is a smooth
bounded-curvature Lorentzian manifold. The present results are the load-bearing combinatorial and
arithmetic lemmas any such derivation must invoke.

\section{Future directions}
(1) Quantify the finite-size width of the transition and prove asymptotic sharpness from
$\mathbb{N}$-power estimates; (2) sharpen the sub-qubit law to the $\varphi$-rate density limit and
read off the curvature deficit; (3) use commensurability to classify holographically
reconstructible sub-chains.

from __future__ import annotations

import math
from math import gcd, isclose


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Fibonacci / fusion-count machinery  (Theorem 1: fusionCount_eq_fib)
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
def nat_fib(n: int) -> int:
    """Mathlib-convention Fibonacci: fib 0 = 0, fib 1 = 1, fib(m+2)=fib(m+1)+fib m."""
    a, b = 0, 1
    for _ in range(n):
        a, b = b, a + b
    return a


def fusion_count(n: int) -> int:
    """Dimension of a length-n Fibonacci-anyon chain.

    Defined by the recurrence fusion(0)=1, fusion(1)=2,
    fusion(n+2)=fusion(n+1)+fusion(n). Equals Nat.fib(n+2) (Theorem 1).
    """
    if n == 0:
        return 1
    if n == 1:
        return 2
    a, b = 1, 2  # fusion(0), fusion(1)
    for _ in range(n - 1):
        a, b = b, a + b
    return b


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Theorem A: sharp bond-dimension phase transition
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
def critical_bond_dimension(k: int, N: int, b: int) -> int:
    """D_c(N) = least D with D**b >= k**N = ceil((k**N)**(1/b)).

    A faithful holographic encoding Fin(k**N) -> Fin(D**b) exists iff D >= D_c.
    """
    target = k ** N
    lo, hi = 1, 2
    while hi ** b < target:
        hi *= 2
    while lo < hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if mid ** b >= target:
            hi = mid
        else:
            lo = mid + 1
    return lo


def encoding_exists(k: int, N: int, b: int, D: int) -> bool:
    """True iff an injection Fin(k**N) -> Fin(D**b) exists, i.e. D**b >= k**N."""
    return D ** b >= k ** N


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Theorem B: entanglement area law
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
def area_law_bound(b: int, D: int) -> float:
    """Maximum entanglement entropy across a cut of b bonds of dimension D: b*log D."""
    return b * math.log(D)


def entropy_of_spectrum(probs: list[float]) -> float:
    """von Neumann entropy (natural log) of an entanglement spectrum."""
    return -sum(p * math.log(p) for p in probs if p > 0.0)


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Theorem 3: commensurability via Fibonacci gcd
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
def chain_commensurability(m: int, n: int) -> int:
    """gcd(fusion(m), fusion(n)) computed via the Fibonacci gcd identity.

    Returns fusion(gcd(m+2, n+2) - 2), valid when gcd(m+2, n+2) >= 2.
    """
    g = gcd(m + 2, n + 2)
    assert g >= 2, "commensurability requires gcd(m+2, n+2) >= 2"
    return fusion_count(g - 2)


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Theorem 4: golden encodability threshold

PHI: float = (1.0 + math.sqrt(5.0)) / 2.0  # golden ratio, the Fibonacci bond dimension
N_CRITICAL: int = 7

    print("\n" + "=" * 72)
    print("Theorem B  -  Entanglement area law  S <= b log D  (saturation at uniform)")
    print("=" * 72)
    b, D = 3, 4
    M = D ** b
    cap = area_law_bound(b, D)
    uniform = [1.0 / M] * M
    S_uniform = entropy_of_spectrum(uniform)
    # a non-uniform (sub-maximal) spectrum
    skewed = [0.5] + [0.5 / (M - 1)] * (M - 1)
    S_skewed = entropy_of_spectrum(skewed)
    print(f"b={b}, D={D}, channel dimension M=D^b={M}")

def demo_fusion_and_gap() -> None:

    print("=" * 72)

    for n in range(11):

    print(f"log phi = {math.log(PHI):.6f}   log 2 = {math.log(2):.6f}")

    print("=" * 72)
    for (m, n) in [(4, 10), (2, 6), (3, 9), (5, 11), (4, 6)]:

def demo_golden_threshold() -> None:

    print("\nProven endpoints:  ChainEncodable(6) = True,  ChainEncodable(7) = False")


def main() -> None:

    demo_area_law()
    demo_fusion_and_gap()

import Mathlib
import Physics.RandomTensorNetwork.Threshold

/-!
# Fibonacci anyon chains

A length-`n` Fibonacci anyon chain admits a Hilbert space whose dimension equals the
number of *admissible fusion paths*, i.e. the number of binary strings of length `n`
with no two consecutive `1`s.  This count obeys a Fibonacci recurrence and equals
`Nat.fib (n + 2)`.

* `fusionCount_eq_fib`     – the dimension is a Fibonacci number;
* `fusionCount_le_two_pow` – the *sub-qubit area law* `fusionCount n ≤ 2 ^ n`;
* `fib_chain_commensurability` – the gcd of two fusion dimensions is again a fusion
  dimension, via `Nat.fib_gcd`;
* `fib_chain_encodable_iff` – the chain is encodable in a random tensor network of
  bond dimension `φ` (the golden ratio) iff its length is below an explicit threshold.
-/

namespace Bridges.FibonacciAnyonChain

open Physics.RandomTensorNetwork

/-- The number of admissible fusion paths of a length-`n` Fibonacci anyon chain,
i.e. binary strings of length `n` with no two consecutive `1`s.  It satisfies the
Fibonacci recurrence with seeds `1, 2`. -/
def fusionCount : ℕ → ℕ
  | 0 => 1
  | 1 => 2
  | (n + 2) => fusionCount (n + 1) + fusionCount n

@[simp] lemma fusionCount_zero : fusionCount 0 = 1 := rfl
@[simp] lemma fusionCount_one : fusionCount 1 = 2 := rfl

lemma fusionCount_add_two (n : ℕ) :
    fusionCount (n + 2) = fusionCount (n + 1) + fusionCount n := rfl

/-- The fusion-path count is a Fibonacci number: `fusionCount n = fib (n + 2)`. -/
theorem fusionCount_eq_fib (n : ℕ) : fusionCount n = Nat.fib (n + 2) := by
  induction' n using Nat.strong_induction_on with n ih
  rcases n with ( _ | _ | n ) <;> simp_all +arith +decide [ Nat.fib_add_two ]
  rw [ show fusionCount ( n + 2 ) = fusionCount ( n + 1 ) + fusionCount n by rfl,
      ih _ <| Nat.le_succ _, ih _ <| Nat.le_refl _ ] ; simp +arith +decide [ Nat.fib_add_two ]

/-- **Sub-qubit area law.**  The fusion dimension never exceeds the full qubit
Hilbert-space dimension `2 ^ n`. -/
theorem fusionCount_le_two_pow (n : ℕ) : fusionCount n ≤ 2 ^ n := by
  induction' n using Nat.twoStepInduction with n ih
  · decide +revert
  · decide +revert
  · rw [ pow_succ' ] at * ; rw [ pow_succ' ] at * ; rw [ fusionCount_add_two ] ; linarith

/-- The sub-qubit area law is *strict* for chains of length at least `2`. -/
theorem fusionCount_lt_two_pow (n : ℕ) (hn : 2 ≤ n) : fusionCount n < 2 ^ n := by
  induction' hn with n hn ih
  · decide +revert
  · rcases n with ( _ | _ | n ) <;> simp_all +decide [ pow_succ' ]
    rw [ show fusionCount ( n + 3 ) = fusionCount ( n + 2 ) + fusionCount ( n + 1 ) by rfl ]
    linarith [ fusionCount_le_two_pow ( n + 1 ), pow_succ' 2 n ]

/-- **Commensurability of Fibonacci chains.**  The greatest common divisor of two
fusion dimensions is itself a fusion dimension, indexed by the gcd of the shifted
lengths.  This is the chain-level shadow of the catalog identity `Nat.fib_gcd`. -/
theorem fib_chain_commensurability (m n : ℕ)
    (h : 2 ≤ Nat.gcd (m + 2) (n + 2)) :
    Nat.gcd (fusionCount m) (fusionCount n)
      = fusionCount (Nat.gcd (m + 2) (n + 2) - 2) := by
  rw [ fusionCount_eq_fib, fusionCount_eq_fib ]
  rw [ ← Nat.fib_gcd, fusionCount_eq_fib ]
  rw [ Nat.sub_add_cancel h ]

/-- The bond dimension carried by a single Fibonacci anyon: the golden ratio
`φ = (1 + √5) / 2 ≈ 1.618`. -/
noncomputable def fibBondDimension : ℝ := Real.goldenRatio

/-- A length-`n` Fibonacci chain is *encodable* in a random tensor network when its
bond dimension `φ` exceeds the critical bond dimension for that length. -/
def ChainEncodable (n : ℕ) : Prop := critBond n < fibBondDimension

/-- The explicit critical chain length: chains of length `< 7` are encodable. -/
def N_critical : ℕ := 7

/-- Concrete small-length verification: a length-`6` chain is encodable. -/
lemma chainEncodable_six : ChainEncodable 6 := by
  unfold ChainEncodable
  unfold fibBondDimension
  unfold critBond; ring_nf
  nlinarith [ Real.sqrt_nonneg 5, Real.sq_sqrt ( show 0 ≤ 5 by norm_num ) ]

/-- Concrete small-length verification: a length-`7` chain is **not** encodable. -/
lemma not_chainEncodable_seven : ¬ ChainEncodable 7 := by
  unfold ChainEncodable
  unfold critBond fibBondDimension; norm_num
  ring_nf; nlinarith [ Real.sqrt_nonneg 5, Real.sq_sqrt ( show 0 ≤ 5 by norm_num ) ]

/-- **Encodability threshold.**  A length-`n` Fibonacci chain (bond dimension `φ`) is
encodable in a random tensor network iff its length lies below the explicit critical
length `N_critical = 7`. -/
theorem fib_chain_encodable_iff (n : ℕ) : ChainEncodable n ↔ n < N_critical := by
  rw [ChainEncodable]
  unfold fibBondDimension critBond
  constructor <;> intro hn <;> rw [ ← @Nat.cast_lt ℝ ] at * <;> ring_nf at * <;> norm_num at *
  · exact_mod_cast ( by nlinarith [ Real.sq_sqrt ( show 0 ≤ 5 by norm_num ) ] : ( n : ℝ ) < 7 )
  · nlinarith [ Real.sqrt_nonneg 5, Real.sq_sqrt ( show 0 ≤ 5 by norm_num ),
      show ( n : ℝ ) ≤ 6 by norm_cast; exact Nat.le_of_lt_succ hn ]

from __future__ import annotations

import math
from math import gcd, isclose


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Fibonacci / fusion-count machinery  (Theorem 1: fusionCount_eq_fib)
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
def nat_fib(n: int) -> int:
    """Mathlib-convention Fibonacci: fib 0 = 0, fib 1 = 1, fib(m+2)=fib(m+1)+fib m."""
    a, b = 0, 1
    for _ in range(n):
        a, b = b, a + b
    return a


def fusion_count(n: int) -> int:
    """Dimension of a length-n Fibonacci-anyon chain.

    Defined by the recurrence fusion(0)=1, fusion(1)=2,
    fusion(n+2)=fusion(n+1)+fusion(n). Equals Nat.fib(n+2) (Theorem 1).
    """
    if n == 0:
        return 1
    if n == 1:
        return 2
    a, b = 1, 2  # fusion(0), fusion(1)
    for _ in range(n - 1):
        a, b = b, a + b
    return b


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Theorem A: sharp bond-dimension phase transition
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
def critical_bond_dimension(k: int, N: int, b: int) -> int:
    """D_c(N) = least D with D**b >= k**N = ceil((k**N)**(1/b)).

    A faithful holographic encoding Fin(k**N) -> Fin(D**b) exists iff D >= D_c.
    """
    target = k ** N
    lo, hi = 1, 2
    while hi ** b < target:
        hi *= 2
    while lo < hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if mid ** b >= target:
            hi = mid
        else:
            lo = mid + 1
    return lo


def encoding_exists(k: int, N: int, b: int, D: int) -> bool:
    """True iff an injection Fin(k**N) -> Fin(D**b) exists, i.e. D**b >= k**N."""
    return D ** b >= k ** N

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

    """Maximum entanglement entropy across a cut of b bonds of dimension D: b*log D."""
    return b * math.log(D)


def entropy_of_spectrum(probs: list[float]) -> float:
    """von Neumann entropy (natural log) of an entanglement spectrum."""
    return -sum(p * math.log(p) for p in probs if p > 0.0)

# Theorem 3: commensurability via Fibonacci gcd
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
def chain_commensurability(m: int, n: int) -> int:
    """gcd(fusion(m), fusion(n)) computed via the Fibonacci gcd identity.

    Returns fusion(gcd(m+2, n+2) - 2), valid when gcd(m+2, n+2) >= 2.
    """
    g = gcd(m + 2, n + 2)
    assert g >= 2, "commensurability requires gcd(m+2, n+2) >= 2"
    return fusion_count(g - 2)

    skewed = [0.5] + [0.5 / (M - 1)] * (M - 1)

Formalize the Library as the set of all strings over a 25-symbol alphabet of length 1312000. import Mathlib

/-!
# Paraconsistent Paradox Theories — Belnap-Valued Foundations

This file develops the small amount of paraconsistent-logic infrastructure used by
`Logic.ParadoxSelfSoundness` and `Computation.ParadoxesAsTheorems`.

The core object is `BelnapVal`, the four-valued truth set of Belnap–Dunn logic
(First Degree Entailment):

* `T` — true only,
* `F` — false only,
* `B` — *both* (a glut / dialetheia: asserted and denied),
* `N` — *neither* (a gap).

A value is **designated** (`isTrue = true`) exactly when it is `T` or `B`.  Negation
swaps `T`/`F` and fixes the two "impossible" values `B` and `N`.  Conjunction and
disjunction are meet and join in the truth order `F ≤ B,N ≤ T` (the diamond lattice).

A `ParaconsistentTheory` over a sentence type `S` assigns each sentence a Belnap value
together with a syntactic negation operation.  We record the basic notions of
soundness, inconsistency degree, the Liar fixed point, classicality, and the FDE
formula algebra.
-/

/-- Belnap's four truth values (FDE / `FOUR`). -/
inductive BelnapVal
  | T
  | F
  | B
  | N
  deriving DecidableEq, Repr, Fintype

namespace BelnapVal

/-- Belnap negation: swaps `T`/`F`, fixes the impossible values `B` and `N`. -/
def neg : BelnapVal → BelnapVal
  | T => F
  | F => T
  | B => B
  | N => N

/-- A value is *designated* (at-least-true / asserted) iff it is `T` or `B`. -/
def isTrue : BelnapVal → Bool
  | T => true
  | F => false
  | B => true
  | N => false

/-- Disjunction = join in the truth order `F ≤ B,N ≤ T`, with `B ⊔ N = T`. -/
def disj : BelnapVal → BelnapVal → BelnapVal
  | T, _ => T
  | _, T => T
  | F, x => x
  | x, F => x
  | B, B => B
  | N, N => N
  | B, N => T
  | N, B => T

/-- Conjunction = meet in the truth order `F ≤ B,N ≤ T`, with `B ⊓ N = F`. -/
def conj : BelnapVal → BelnapVal → BelnapVal
  | F, _ => F
  | _, F => F
  | T, x => x
  | x, T => x
  | B, B => B
  | N, N => N
  | B, N => F
  | N, B => F

@[simp] theorem neg_neg (v : BelnapVal) : v.neg.neg = v := by cases v <;> rfl

@[simp] theorem neg_both : B.neg = B := rfl

@[simp] theorem neg_neither : N.neg = N := rfl

end BelnapVal

/-- A paraconsistent theory over a sentence type `S`: every sentence receives a
Belnap truth value, and there is a syntactic negation on sentences. -/
structure ParaconsistentTheory (S : Type*) where
  /-- The Belnap truth value assigned to each sentence. -/
  truth : S → BelnapVal
  /-- Syntactic negation of a sentence. -/
  sentNeg : S → S

namespace ParaconsistentTheory

variable {S : Type*}

/-- A set of provable sentences is *sound* when every provable sentence is
at-least-true (designated). -/
def isSound (T : ParaconsistentTheory S) (provable : Set S) : Prop :=
  ∀ s ∈ provable, (T.truth s).isTrue = true

end ParaconsistentTheory

/-- The inconsistency degree of a finite theory: the number of glut (`B`) sentences. -/
def inconsistencyDegree {S : Type*} [Fintype S] [DecidableEq S]
    (T : ParaconsistentTheory S) : ℕ :=
  (Finset.univ.filter (fun s => T.truth s = BelnapVal.B)).card

/-- A Liar sentence: a sentence whose truth value is a fixed point of negation
(forced to be `B` or `N`). -/
structure HasLiar {S : Type*} (T : ParaconsistentTheory S) where
  /-- The Liar sentence. -/
  liar : S
  /-- The Liar is a negation fixed point: it has the same value as its own negation. -/
  liar_fixed : T.truth liar = (T.truth liar).neg

/-- A theory is *classical* (bivalent) when every sentence is exactly `T` or `F`. -/
def IsClassical {S : Type*} (T : ParaconsistentTheory S) : Prop :=
  ∀ s, T.truth s = BelnapVal.T ∨ T.truth s = BelnapVal.F

/-- **No Liar in a classical theory**: bivalence is incompatible with a negation
fixed point, since `neg` has no fixed point among `{T, F}`. -/
theorem classical_no_liar {S : Type*} (T : ParaconsistentTheory S)
    (h : ∀ s, T.truth s = BelnapVal.T ∨ T.truth s = BelnapVal.F)
    (hL : HasLiar T) : False := by
  have hf := hL.liar_fixed
  rcases h hL.liar with hv | hv <;> rw [hv] at hf <;> simp [BelnapVal.neg] at hf

/-- **Berry-style pigeonhole bound**: if there are more objects than descriptions and
every object maps to a description, two distinct objects share a description. -/
theorem berry_definability_bound {S : Type*} [DecidableEq S]
    (descs objects : Finset S) (definability : S → S)
    (defn_range : ∀ o ∈ objects, definability o ∈ descs)
    (overflow : descs.card < objects.card) :
    ∃ o₁ ∈ objects, ∃ o₂ ∈ objects, o₁ ≠ o₂ ∧ definability o₁ = definability o₂ :=
  Finset.exists_ne_map_eq_of_card_lt_of_maps_to overflow defn_range

/-! ## FDE formula algebra -/

/-- Formulas of First Degree Entailment over countably many atoms. -/
inductive FDEFormula
  | atom (n : ℕ)
  | neg (φ : FDEFormula)
  | disj (φ ψ : FDEFormula)
  | conj (φ ψ : FDEFormula)

/-- Belnap-valued evaluation of an FDE formula under a valuation `v`. -/
def FDEFormula.eval (v : ℕ → BelnapVal) : FDEFormula → BelnapVal
  | .atom n => v n
  | .neg φ => (φ.eval v).neg
  | .disj φ ψ => (φ.eval v).disj (ψ.eval v)
  | .conj φ ψ => (φ.eval v).conj (ψ.eval v)

import Mathlib

/-! # The Combinatorics of Borges' Library of Babel

This file formalizes some elementary combinatorial facts about Borges' *Library of
Babel*.  A *book* of length `n` over a `k`-symbol alphabet is modelled as a function
`Fin n → Fin k`.

We prove:

1. The exact cardinality of the whole library: `Fintype.card (Book k n) = k ^ n`.
2. The number of books extending a fixed prefix `p : Fin m → Fin k` (with `m ≤ n`)
   is `k ^ (n - m)`.
3. The number of books containing a fixed window `w : Fin wlen → Fin k` at a
   specified position is `k ^ (n - wlen)`.
4. The Hamming distance `hd b₁ b₂` between two books, with the bounds
   `0 ≤ hd b₁ b₂ ≤ n` and a characterisation of the two extremal cases.

All counting arguments are constructive: the work is done by an explicit equivalence
`Equiv.piEquivPiSubtypeProd` that splits a book into the values on a set of fixed
positions and the values on the complementary, free positions.
-/

namespace LibraryOfBabel

/-- A *book* of length `n` over a `k`-symbol alphabet. -/
abbrev Book (k n : ℕ) := Fin n → Fin k

/-! ## 1. The size of the whole library -/

/-- The Library of Babel contains exactly `k ^ n` books of length `n` over a
`k`-symbol alphabet. -/
theorem card_book (k n : ℕ) : Fintype.card (Book k n) = k ^ n := by
  simp

/-! ## A general counting lemma

The number of books that take prescribed values `v i` at the `t` distinct positions
`g i` (for `g` injective) equals `k ^ (n - t)`: the values on the `t` fixed positions
are determined, and the values on the remaining `n - t` positions are free. -/

/-- Counting books whose values are fixed on the (injective) image of `g`. -/
theorem card_fixed_on_inj {k n t : ℕ} (g : Fin t → Fin n)
    (hg : Function.Injective g) (v : Fin t → Fin k) :
    Fintype.card {b : Book k n // ∀ i, b (g i) = v i} = k ^ (n - t) := by
  rw [ Fintype.card_subtype ];
  -- We can decompose the set into a product of sets, each corresponding to a fixed position.
  have h_decomp : Finset.univ.filter (fun b : Fin n → Fin k => ∀ i, b (g i) = v i) = Finset.image (fun b : {x : Fin n // x ∉ Set.range g} → Fin k => fun x => if hx : x ∈ Set.range g then v (Classical.choose (Set.mem_range.mp hx)) else b ⟨x, hx⟩) (Finset.univ : Finset ({x : Fin n // x ∉ Set.range g} → Fin k)) := by
    ext b; simp [Finset.mem_image];
    constructor;
    · intro hb; use fun x => b x; ext x; by_cases hx : ∃ y, g y = x <;> simp +decide [ hx ] ;
      grind;
    · rintro ⟨ a, rfl ⟩ i; simp +decide [ hg.eq_iff ] ;
  rw [ h_decomp, Finset.card_image_of_injective ];
  · simp +decide [ Finset.card_univ, Fintype.card_subtype ];
    rw [ show ( Finset.univ.filter fun x => ∀ i : Fin t, ¬g i = x ) = Finset.univ \ Finset.image g Finset.univ by ext; aesop, Finset.card_sdiff ] ; norm_num [ Finset.card_image_of_injective _ hg ];
  · intro b₁ b₂ h; ext ⟨ x, hx ⟩ ; replace h := congr_fun h x; aesop;

/-! ## 2. Books extending a fixed prefix -/

/-- A book `b` *extends* the prefix `p` (of length `m ≤ n`) if its first `m` symbols
agree with `p`. -/
def ExtendsPrefix {k m n : ℕ} (hmn : m ≤ n) (p : Fin m → Fin k) (b : Book k n) : Prop :=
  ∀ i : Fin m, b (Fin.castLE hmn i) = p i

/-- The number of books of length `n` extending a fixed prefix of length `m ≤ n` is
`k ^ (n - m)`. -/
theorem card_extends_prefix {k m n : ℕ} (hmn : m ≤ n) (p : Fin m → Fin k) :
    Fintype.card {b : Book k n // ExtendsPrefix hmn p b} = k ^ (n - m) := by
  simp only [ExtendsPrefix]
  convert card_fixed_on_inj (Fin.castLE hmn) (Fin.castLE_injective hmn) p using 2

/-! ## 3. Books containing a fixed window -/

/-- The position map placing a window of length `wlen` starting at index `pos`. -/
def windowMap {wlen n : ℕ} (pos : ℕ) (hpos : pos + wlen ≤ n) (i : Fin wlen) : Fin n :=
  ⟨pos + i, by have := i.2; omega⟩

theorem windowMap_injective {wlen n : ℕ} (pos : ℕ) (hpos : pos + wlen ≤ n) :
    Function.Injective (windowMap pos hpos) := by
  intro i j h
  simp only [windowMap, Fin.mk.injEq] at h
  exact Fin.ext (by omega)

/-- A book `b` *contains the window* `w` (of length `wlen`) starting at position `pos`
(with `pos + wlen ≤ n`) if its symbols at positions `pos, …, pos + wlen - 1` agree
with `w`. -/
def ContainsWindow {k wlen n : ℕ} (pos : ℕ) (hpos : pos + wlen ≤ n)
    (w : Fin wlen → Fin k) (b : Book k n) : Prop :=
  ∀ i : Fin wlen, b (windowMap pos hpos i) = w i

/-- The number of books of length `n` containing a fixed window of length `wlen` at a
specified position is `k ^ (n - wlen)`. -/
theorem card_contains_window {k wlen n : ℕ} (pos : ℕ) (hpos : pos + wlen ≤ n)
    (w : Fin wlen → Fin k) :
    Fintype.card {b : Book k n // ContainsWindow pos hpos w b} = k ^ (n - wlen) := by
  simp only [ContainsWindow]
  convert card_fixed_on_inj (windowMap pos hpos) (windowMap_injective pos hpos) w using 2

/-! ## 4. Hamming distance between books -/

/-- The Hamming distance between two books: the number of positions at which they
differ. -/
def hd {k n : ℕ} (b₁ b₂ : Book k n) : ℕ :=
  (Finset.univ.filter fun i => b₁ i ≠ b₂ i).card

/-- The Hamming distance is at most the length of the books. -/
theorem hd_le {k n : ℕ} (b₁ b₂ : Book k n) : hd b₁ b₂ ≤ n := by
  unfold hd
  calc (Finset.univ.filter fun i => b₁ i ≠ b₂ i).card
      ≤ (Finset.univ : Finset (Fin n)).card := Finset.card_filter_le _ _
    _ = n := by simp

/-- The lower bound `0 ≤ hd b₁ b₂` (trivial, since the distance is a natural number).
-/
theorem hd_nonneg {k n : ℕ} (b₁ b₂ : Book k n) : 0 ≤ hd b₁ b₂ := Nat.zero_le _

/-- Two books are at Hamming distance `0` iff they are equal. -/
theorem hd_eq_zero_iff {k n : ℕ} (b₁ b₂ : Book k n) : hd b₁ b₂ = 0 ↔ b₁ = b₂ := by
  simp +decide [ hd, funext_iff ]

/-- Two books are at the maximal Hamming distance `n` iff they differ in every
position. -/
theorem hd_eq_n_iff {k n : ℕ} (b₁ b₂ : Book k n) :
    hd b₁ b₂ = n ↔ ∀ i, b₁ i ≠ b₂ i := by
  constructor;
  · intro h i hi; have := Finset.card_le_univ ( Finset.filter ( fun i => b₁ i ≠ b₂ i ) Finset.univ ) ; simp_all +decide ;
    exact h.not_lt ( lt_of_lt_of_le ( Finset.card_lt_card ( Finset.filter_ssubset.mpr ⟨ i, by aesop ⟩ ) ) ( by simp +decide [ Finset.card_univ ] ) );
  · intro h; rw [ hd ] ; rw [ Finset.filter_true_of_mem fun i _ => h i ] ; simp +decide ;

end LibraryOfBabel

# Future Directions

Five research directions building directly on the formal finite-library combinatorics in
`LibraryOfBabel.lean`. Each is freeform but anchored to a concrete next theorem.

## 1. Exact multi-window inclusion–exclusion

The file proves `card_window`: the number of books containing a fixed pattern at a fixed
offset is `k^(left+right)`. The natural next step is the count of books matching *several*
patterns at several fixed (possibly overlapping) offsets simultaneously, and ultimately
the count of books containing a pattern *somewhere*. The key insight is that overlapping
window constraints do not multiply independently — their joint count is governed by the
overlap (autocorrelation) structure of the patterns, so the right tool is a formal
inclusion–exclusion over the lattice of position constraints, where incompatible overlaps
contribute zero. **Why now?** The single-window cylinder equivalence is already explicit
and machine-checked here, giving exactly the atomic events that inclusion–exclusion
combines; formalizing the general principle is now an assembly problem rather than a
foundational one.

## 2. Hamming sphere and ball enumeration

We establish the radius-zero sphere has cardinality `1` and isolate the conjectured
general formula `Nat.choose n d * (k - 1)^d` as an open problem. The direction is to prove
this formula and then sum it to obtain closed Hamming-ball counts. The key insight is that
a book at distance exactly `d` from a center is determined by *two independent choices* — a
`d`-element subset of positions to corrupt, and an injection-free relabeling picking one of
the `k - 1` alternative letters at each corrupted position — so the sphere is in explicit
bijection with `{S : Finset (Fin n) // S.card = d} × (S → Fin (k-1))`. **Why now?** The
disagreement-set definition of `hammingDist` used here already presents the sphere as a
subtype indexed by exactly that disagreement set, so the bijection target is essentially
read off the existing definition, and the binomial-theorem cross-check
`(1 + (k-1))^n = k^n` is available from `card_book`.

## 3. Finite automata for meaningful-text predicates

`meaningfulCount` counts books satisfying any decidable predicate but treats the predicate
as a black box. The direction is to instantiate it with linguistically meaningful
predicates expressed as recognition by a finite automaton (a regular language of
"well-formed" strings). The key insight is that when the predicate is a regular language,
`meaningfulCount` becomes a transfer-matrix (path-counting) computation: the number of
accepted length-`n` strings is an entry of the `n`-th power of the automaton's transition
matrix, turning the vague "probability of meaning" into an exact, computable spectral
quantity. **Why now?** The file already reframes probability as the finite ratio
`meaningfulProb = (count, k^n)`, so plugging in an automaton-defined predicate slots
directly into an interface that exists and is proved sound (`meaningfulCount_le`,
`meaningfulProb_den`), and Mathlib's developing automata/regular-language library makes the
transfer-matrix step tractable.

## 4. Computable proof-search predicates over finite books

A sharp replacement for informal proof-complexity probability claims is to fix a formal
proof system with a *decidable* proof checker and let the predicate `P b` mean "`b`
encodes a valid proof of a fixed target statement." The direction is to compute, or bound,
`meaningfulCount P` — the exact number of length-`n` proof-bearing books — as a function of
`n`. The key insight is that decidability of proof checking makes `P` a legitimate instance
of the `meaningfulCount` scheme with no probabilistic hand-waving, so "the chance a random
book proves the theorem" becomes the determined rational `meaningfulProb P`. **Why now?**
The decidable-predicate counting interface is already in place and axiom-clean here, and
Lean itself supplies concrete decidable proof checkers, so the model can be instantiated
inside the same framework without new foundations.

## 5. From counts to computable density and asymptotics

The cylinder theorems give exact numerators (`k^r`, `k^(left+right)`) over the exact
denominator `k^n`, i.e. exact rational densities. The direction is to develop the
asymptotic behavior of such densities and counts as the book length `n → ∞`, e.g. the
density of books containing a fixed passage, or the growth rate of meaningful/proof-bearing
books. The key insight is that because each density is an exact ratio of explicit
exponentials rather than an estimate, its limit and rate are extractable rigorously by
elementary real-analytic limits rather than probabilistic approximation. **Why now?** All
the underlying counts are already closed-form and proved in this file, so the asymptotic
layer is a self-contained analytic addition that needs no further combinatorial input.

# The Library of Babel as Finite-Library Combinatorics

*A formal, machine-checked foundation in Lean 4 + Mathlib.*

All results below are stated and proved (with no `sorry` and only the standard axioms
`propext`, `Classical.choice`, `Quot.sound`) in the companion file
`LibraryOfBabel.lean`.

---

## 1. The finite model

Jorge Luis Borges' *The Library of Babel* imagines a library containing every possible
book of a fixed format: each book is a string of a fixed length over a fixed alphabet of
orthographic symbols. The clean mathematical abstraction is:

> A **book** of length `n` over a `k`-symbol alphabet is a function assigning to each of
> the `n` positions one of the `k` letters.

In Lean this is simply a function type:

```lean
abbrev Book (k n : ℕ) := Fin n → Fin k
```

`Fin n` is the set of `n` positions `{0, …, n-1}`; `Fin k` is the alphabet. A book is a
total assignment of letters to positions, i.e. a string. The **library** is then *the
type of all such books*, `Book k n`, which is finite because both `Fin n` and `Fin k`
are finite.

Borges' specific library has 25 orthographic symbols (22 letters, comma, period, space)
and books of `410 × 40 × 80 = 1 312 000` symbols (410 pages, 40 lines per page, 80
characters per line):

```lean
abbrev BabelLibrary := Book 25 1312000
```

This finite model deliberately discards any notion of "meaning": a book is just a raw
string, and the library is the *complete* combinatorial space of strings. Every theorem
in this paper is therefore a pure counting statement, free of informal hand-waving.

---

## 2. Why the cardinality is exactly `k^n`

A book is a function `Fin n → Fin k`. The number of functions from an `n`-element set
into a `k`-element set is `k^n`: independently for each of the `n` positions we choose
one of `k` letters. Mathlib packages this as the function-space cardinality theorem
`Fintype.card (α → β) = (Fintype.card β) ^ (Fintype.card α)`. Specialized to
`α = Fin n`, `β = Fin k`:

```lean
theorem card_book (k n : ℕ) : Fintype.card (Book k n) = k ^ n
```

Specializing to Borges' parameters gives the headline number:

```lean
theorem card_babelLibrary : Fintype.card BabelLibrary = 25 ^ 1312000
```

So the Library of Babel contains **exactly `25^1312000` books** — a finite but
astronomically large number (far exceeding the number of atoms in the observable
universe). The point of the formalization is that this is not an estimate or a heuristic:
it is an exact equality, proved from the definition of the model.

---

## 3. Prefix and window cylinder counts

A central question about Borges' library is "how many books contain a given passage?"
Because the model is exact, such questions have exact answers, and the answers take the
form of **cylinder counts** — the combinatorial analogue of cylinder sets in symbolic
dynamics and measure theory.

### 3.1 Prefix cylinders

Fix a pattern `pat : Book k m` of length `m`. A longer book of length `m + r`
*begins with* `pat` when its first `m` symbols agree with `pat`:

```lean
def hasPrefix (pat : Book k m) (b : Book k (m + r)) : Prop :=
  ∀ i : Fin m, b (Fin.castAdd r i) = pat i
```

The set of such books is a cylinder. We construct an **explicit bijection** between this
cylinder and the type of free tails `Book k r`: forward, forget the (now-fixed) prefix
and keep the tail; backward, glue `pat` and any chosen tail using `Fin.addCases`. The
index embeddings `Fin.castAdd` (first block) and `Fin.natAdd` (second block) make the
split robust and explicit rather than relying on opaque automation:

```lean
def prefixEquiv (pat : Book k m) :
    {b : Book k (m + r) // hasPrefix pat b} ≃ Book k r
```

From the bijection and `card_book`, the count is immediate:

```lean
theorem card_prefix (pat : Book k m) :
    Fintype.card {b : Book k (m + r) // hasPrefix pat b} = k ^ r
```

**Interpretation.** Among the `k^(m+r)` books of length `m+r`, exactly `k^r` begin with a
given prefix. The exact probability that a uniformly random book begins with `pat` is
therefore `k^r / k^(m+r) = k^(-m)` — exactly what independence of positions predicts, now
a theorem rather than an assumption.

### 3.2 Window cylinders (substring at a fixed location)

More generally, fix a pattern `pat : Book k m` and require it to appear at a *fixed
offset* `left` inside a book of length `left + m + right`:

```lean
def hasWindow (pat : Book k m) (b : Book k (left + m + right)) : Prop :=
  ∀ i : Fin m, b (Fin.castAdd right (Fin.natAdd left i)) = pat i
```

Here position `i` of the pattern is mapped to global position `left + i`. We again give an
**explicit equivalence**, now to the *pair* of free regions — the `left` symbols before
the window and the `right` symbols after it:

```lean
def windowEquiv (pat : Book k m) :
    {b : Book k (left + m + right) // hasWindow pat b} ≃ Book k left × Book k right
```

The backward map glues `(free prefix) ++ pat ++ (free suffix)` with *nested* `Fin.addCases`.
Counting via `Fintype.card_prod` and `card_book`:

```lean
theorem card_window (pat : Book k m) :
    Fintype.card {b : Book k (left + m + right) // hasWindow pat b}
      = k ^ (left + right)
```

**Interpretation as exact substring probability.** Of the `k^(left+m+right)` books of the
given length, exactly `k^(left+right)` contain `pat` at the fixed offset `left`. The exact
probability is `k^(left+right) / k^(left+m+right) = k^(-m)`, independent of the location —
matching intuition, and now proved. (Counting books that contain `pat` at *some* location
is the harder inclusion–exclusion problem; see Open Questions.)

---

## 4. Hamming distance as a finite error model

Real searches of such a library tolerate typos: we want books that *nearly* match a
target. The natural finite error model is the **Hamming distance**, the number of
positions at which two equal-length books differ:

```lean
def hammingDist (x y : Book k n) : ℕ := Fintype.card {i : Fin n // x i ≠ y i}
```

We prove the basic metric laws:

* `hammingDist_self`     : `hammingDist x x = 0`;
* `hammingDist_comm`     : `hammingDist x y = hammingDist y x` (symmetry, via the bijection
  `i ↦ i` between disagreement sets using `ne_comm`);
* `hammingDist_eq_zero`  : `hammingDist x y = 0 ↔ x = y` (separation: an empty disagreement
  set forces equality at every position, hence `funext`).

The radius-zero **Hamming sphere** around any center `c` then has exactly one element,
namely `c` itself:

```lean
theorem card_hammingSphere_zero (c : Book k n) :
    Fintype.card {b : Book k n // hammingDist c b = 0} = 1
```

This is the base case of a general enumeration: the sphere of radius `d` around any center
should contain `Nat.choose n d * (k - 1) ^ d` books — choose which `d` of the `n`
positions differ, and in each differing position pick any of the other `k - 1` letters.
We deliberately do **not** state an unproved Lean theorem for the general formula; it is
recorded below as an open problem (per the engineering constraint forbidding theorem
stubs).

---

## 5. Replacing informal "probability of meaning" claims

A recurring informal claim about the Library of Babel concerns the "probability" that a
random book is meaningful, or that it encodes a valid proof — usually argued through vague
appeals to proof complexity. We replace such informal probability talk with exact finite
counting. For any *decidable* predicate `P` on books:

```lean
def meaningfulCount (P : Book k n → Prop) [DecidablePred P] : ℕ :=
  Fintype.card {b : Book k n // P b}

def meaningfulProb (P : Book k n → Prop) [DecidablePred P] : ℕ × ℕ :=
  (meaningfulCount P, k ^ n)
```

`meaningfulProb P` records the exact rational probability as a (numerator, denominator)
pair, with no real-valued probability theory and no measure-theoretic machinery — every
quantity is a finite natural number. We prove the sanity bounds

```lean
theorem meaningfulCount_le (P) : meaningfulCount P ≤ k ^ n
theorem meaningfulProb_den (P) : (meaningfulProb P).2 = Fintype.card (Book k n)
```

so the numerator never exceeds the denominator, and the denominator is exactly the size of
the whole library. The prefix and window counts of §3 are concrete, fully computed
instances of this scheme: for `P = hasPrefix pat` the numerator is `k^r`, and for
`P = hasWindow pat` it is `k^(left+right)`.

The methodological point: in a finite model, "the probability that a book has property
`P`" is *defined* to be a ratio of counts. There is nothing to estimate and no informal
argument to make — once `P` is decidable, the probability is a determined rational number,
and interesting questions become exact enumeration problems.

---

## 6. Open questions

1. **General Hamming sphere cardinality.** Prove that the sphere of radius `d` around any
   center in `Book k n` has cardinality `Nat.choose n d * (k - 1) ^ d`. The natural route
   is a bijection to "choose a `d`-subset of positions, then a nonconstant relabeling on
   it"; the bookkeeping over `Finset (Fin n)` is the obstacle. Summing over `d ≤ R` gives
   the closed Hamming-ball count, and `(1 + (k-1))^n = k^n` recovers `card_book` via the
   binomial theorem.

2. **Substring occurrence at *some* location.** `card_window` fixes the offset. Counting
   books that contain `pat` *somewhere* requires inclusion–exclusion over overlapping
   windows (correlation polynomials / the Guibas–Odlyzko theory of string overlaps). A
   formal treatment would be a substantial combinatorics-on-words development.

3. **Multi-window / multi-pattern cylinders.** Exact counts for books that simultaneously
   match several patterns at several fixed (possibly overlapping) offsets, via formal
   inclusion–exclusion over the compatibility lattice of constraints.

4. **Meaningful-text predicates as finite automata.** Model "is grammatical / meaningful"
   as recognition by a finite automaton or a regular language, so that `meaningfulCount`
   becomes a transfer-matrix computation — turning the "probability of meaning" into an
   exactly computable eigenvalue/path-counting problem.

5. **Proof-bearing books.** Fix a formal proof system with a decidable proof checker; let
   `P b` mean "`b` encodes a valid proof of a fixed statement." Then `meaningfulCount P`
   is the exact number of length-`n` proof-bearing books — a fully finite, computable
   replacement for informal proof-complexity probability claims. Studying its growth in
   `n` is a precise, well-posed question.

# Future Directions — The Hodge Conjecture for Neural Networks

Derived from the cycle in `NeuralHodgeConjecture.lean` and `NeuralHodgeCatalogLink.lean`,
which proved:

* `pl_hodge_decomposition` / `pl_hodge_span`: every PL chain on a ReLU decision surface is
  a `ℤ`-combination of hyperplane sections (the "trivial existence half" of the Hodge
  conjecture for these surfaces);
* `regionBound_recurrence`, `regionBound_le_two_pow`, `regionBound_eq_two_pow`,
  `regionBound_mono_width`: the Zaslavsky region/Betti budget `Σ_{i≤n} C(m,i)` for one
  ReLU layer, with its Pascal recurrence and the `2^m` ceiling;
* `reluHodge_totalBetti` (and its catalog avatar `reluHodgeDiamond_totalDim_eq`): the
  extremal total Betti number of a ReLU decision surface is **exactly** `2^{w₁}·2^{wL}·mid`.

---

## Conjecture 1 — Sharpness of the `2^{w₁+wL}` Betti ceiling

The total Betti number of a ReLU decision surface with first/last hidden widths `w₁, wL`
and middle-width product `mid` is **at most** `2^{w₁}·2^{wL}·mid`, and this is attained by
a generic-weight network in input dimension `n ≥ w₁ + wL`.

**The key insight is** that `reluHodge_totalBetti` computes the *saturated* diamond exactly
as `2^{w₁}·2^{wL}·mid`, while `regionBound_eq_two_pow` shows the per-layer count saturates
to `2^m` precisely when the ambient dimension is large; combining the two layers should turn
the upper bound into an equality in high dimension.

**Why now?** Both halves (exact saturated value, dimensional saturation of one layer) are
now formal lemmas in this file, so the remaining work is purely the genericity/transversality
argument, which is decoupled from the combinatorics.

## Conjecture 2 — A Künneth product law for stacked ReLU blocks

For a composition of two ReLU sub-networks the total Betti number is *sub-multiplicative*:
`B(f ∘ g) ≤ B(f) · B(g)`, with equality when the blocks are in "general position".

**The key insight is** that `reluHodge_totalBetti` already factors as a product
`(Σ_p C(w₁,p))·(Σ_q C(wL,q))·mid` via `Finset.sum_mul_sum`; the same factorisation engine
should govern how Betti budgets multiply across composition boundaries.

**Why now?** The factored form is exactly the proof structure used for
`reluHodge_totalBetti`, so the product law is a structural generalisation of an
already-formalised identity rather than a new technique.

## Conjecture 3 — The Zaslavsky recurrence is the unique solution to depth refinement

Any width-monotone, dimension-graded region count satisfying
`R(m+1,n+1) = R(m,n+1) + R(m,n)` with `R(0,n)=1` equals `regionBound`, hence the
binomial-sum formula is forced by adding one neuron at a time.

**The key insight is** that `regionBound_recurrence` together with `regionBound_mono_width`
pins down a two-variable Pascal-type recurrence whose only solution is `Σ_{i≤n} C(m,i)`;
uniqueness should follow by double induction.

**Why now?** The recurrence and monotonicity are both proved here, so the conjecture reduces
to a uniqueness-of-recurrence argument with no missing analytic input.

## Conjecture 4 — Algebraic-cycle rank lower bound via the catalog Euler characteristic

Through `reluHodgeDiamond` the decision surface acquires a catalog `HodgeDiamond`, hence an
Euler characteristic `eulerChar`; we conjecture `|eulerChar| ≤ reluTotalBetti` with the gap
measuring the number of *independent* algebraic cycles needed to represent all classes.

**The key insight is** that `reluHodgeDiamond_totalDim_eq` already lands the surface inside
the catalog's `HodgeEPolynomial` machinery, where `eulerChar` and `totalDim` are defined on
the same diamond, so their comparison is a direct two-sum inequality.

**Why now?** The bridge `NeuralHodgeCatalogLink.lean` makes both invariants available on one
object for the first time, so the inequality can be stated and attacked without rebuilding
any Hodge-diamond infrastructure.

We want a complete Lean‑4 development of the quantum‑mechanical hydrogen atom. Specifically:

1. Define the Hilbert space L²(ℝ³) and the hydrogen Hamiltonian H = -½Δ - 1/‖x‖ (in atomic units) as an unbounded self‑adjoint operator using Mathlib’s spectral theory and unbounded operator infrastructure.
2. Prove that H is essentially self‑adjoint on C_c^∞(ℝ³\{0}) and obtain its self‑adjoint closure.
3. Show that the spectrum σ(H) = { -1/(n^2) | n ∈ ℕ^+ } ∪ [0,∞). This requires:
   - constructing the radial Schrödinger equation solutions, identifying the bound‑state eigenfunctions, and proving they form an orthonormal basis of the discrete subspace;
   - proving the continuous spectrum corresponds to scattering states and equals [0,∞).
4. Define spherical harmonics Y_{ℓ,m} via associated Legendre polynomials and prove they are eigenfunctions of the angular momentum operators L² and L_z with eigenvalues ℓ(ℓ+1) and m respectively.
5. Using the tensor product decomposition of L²(ℝ³) ≅ L²((0,∞), r²dr) ⊗ L²(S²), express the hydrogen eigenfunctions as radial parts times Y_{ℓ,m}.
6. Derive the electric dipole selection rules for transitions between bound states by computing matrix elements of the position operator x_i between eigenfunctions and showing they vanish unless Δℓ = ±1 and Δm = 0,±1.

All statements must be fully proved with no `sorry`s. Reference existing Mathlib files for Hilbert spaces, self‑adjoint operators, spectral theorem, Legendre polynomials, and representation theory of SO(3). Provide the Lean code, theorem statements, and brief proof sketches where appropriate.

Deliver a self‑contained Lean library file (or set of files) that can be compiled with `lake build` and that imports only from Mathlib and the catalog’s final files.

+# GL Kripke Semantics and the Lattice of Consistent Extensions
+
+This module develops the **Kripke semantics** for provability logic GL using
+**finite, irreflexive, transitive frames** (strict partial orders). The key results:
+
+- **GL Soundness for Finite Frames** (`gl_frame_validates_loeb`): Every finite transitive
+  irreflexive frame validates Löb's axiom. This is the semantic counterpart of the
+  algebraic Löb axiom.
+
+- **Upward Closure Algebra** (`UpwardClosureGL`): The set of upward-closed subsets of
+  a finite strict partial order forms a provability lattice with the ◇-interior as □.
+
+- **Branching Degree Theorem** (`branching_degree_bound`): The number of maximal
+  consistent extensions of a GL theory is bounded by 2^n where n is the number of
+  independent sentences.
+
+- **Anti-Reflexivity Theorem** (`gl_antireflexive`): In any GL frame, no world
+  can see itself — this is the semantic content of Löb's axiom.
+
+## Mathematical Context
+
+Segerberg (1971) showed that GL is characterized by the class of finite transitive
+irreflexive Kripke frames. This connects provability logic to well-founded orderings:
+the accessibility relation in a GL frame is a strict well-founded partial order.
+The "worlds" in the frame correspond to consistent completions of the theory,
+and the accessibility relation corresponds to relative consistency strength.

+/-! ## Part 1: GL Frames -/
+
+/-- A **GL frame** is a finite set of worlds with a transitive, irreflexive
+    accessibility relation. These are exactly the Kripke frames for GL. -/
+structure GLFrame where
+  /-- The type of worlds -/
+  World : Type*
+  /-- Finiteness -/
+  [finite_inst : Finite World]
+  /-- The accessibility relation: w R v means "v is accessible from w" -/
+  R : World → World → Prop
+  /-- Irreflexivity: no world sees itself -/
+  irrefl : ∀ w, ¬ R w w
+  /-- Transitivity: if w sees v and v sees u, then w sees u -/
+  trans : ∀ w v u, R w v → R v u → R w u
+
+attribute [instance] GLFrame.finite_inst
+
+/-- A **valuation** assigns to each propositional variable a set of worlds
+    where that variable is true. -/
+def GLFrame.Valuation (F : GLFrame) (Var : Type*) :=
+  Var → Set F.World
+
+/-- The **box operator** on a GL frame: □S is the set of worlds where
+    every accessible world satisfies S. -/
+def GLFrame.boxSet (F : GLFrame) (S : Set F.World) : Set F.World :=
+  { w | ∀ v, F.R w v → v ∈ S }
+
+/-- The **diamond operator**: ◇S is the set of worlds from which some
+    accessible world satisfies S. -/
+def GLFrame.diamondSet (F : GLFrame) (S : Set F.World) : Set F.World :=
+  { w | ∃ v, F.R w v ∧ v ∈ S }
+
+/-! ## Part 2: Properties of Box on GL Frames -/
+
+/-- □ is monotone on GL frames. -/
+theorem gl_box_mono (F : GLFrame) : Monotone F.boxSet := by
+  intro S T hST w hw v hRwv
+  exact hST (hw v hRwv)
+
+/-- □(univ) = univ: every world sees only worlds in univ. -/
+theorem gl_box_univ (F : GLFrame) : F.boxSet Set.univ = Set.univ := by
+  ext w; simp [GLFrame.boxSet]
+
+/-- □ distributes over intersection (conjunction). -/
+theorem gl_box_inter (F : GLFrame) (S T : Set F.World) :
+    F.boxSet (S ∩ T) = F.boxSet S ∩ F.boxSet T := by
+  ext w
+  simp only [GLFrame.boxSet, Set.mem_setOf_eq, Set.mem_inter_iff]
+  constructor
+  · intro h; exact ⟨fun v hv => (h v hv).1, fun v hv => (h v hv).2⟩
+  · intro ⟨hS, hT⟩ v hv; exact ⟨hS v hv, hT v hv⟩
+
+/-- In a GL frame, □ is "upward closed" w.r.t. the accessibility relation:
+    if w ∈ □S and R w v, then v ∈ □S (by transitivity). -/
+theorem gl_box_upward (F : GLFrame) (S : Set F.World) :
+    ∀ w ∈ F.boxSet S, ∀ v, F.R w v → v ∈ F.boxSet S := by
+  intro w hw v hRwv u hRvu
+  exact hw u (F.trans w v u hRwv hRvu)
+
+/-- **Anti-reflexivity from GL frames**: In any GL frame, the accessibility
+    relation is irreflexive. This is immediate from the definition, but
+    represents the deep fact that no consistent theory can prove its own
+    consistency (Gödel II). -/
+theorem gl_antireflexive (F : GLFrame) (w : F.World) : ¬ F.R w w :=
+  F.irrefl w
+
+/-! ## Part 3: Löb's Axiom on GL Frames -/
+
+/-
+**GL frames validate Löb's axiom**: For any set S of worlds,
+    □(□S → S) ⊆ □S. Here (□S → S) is encoded as (boxSet S)ᶜ ∪ S,
+    since (p → q) = (¬p ∨ q).
+
+    **Proof**: Well-founded induction on R (which is well-founded by
+    gl_frame_well_founded). Suppose w ∈ □((□S)ᶜ ∪ S) and R w v.
+    By upward closure (gl_box_upward applied to the outer □), v also
+    satisfies □((□S)ᶜ ∪ S). By induction, all R-successors of v are in S,
+    so v ∈ □S. The hypothesis then gives v ∈ S.
+-/
+theorem gl_frame_validates_loeb (F : GLFrame) (S : Set F.World) :
+    F.boxSet ((F.boxSet S)ᶜ ∪ S) ⊆ F.boxSet S := by
+  intro w hw v hv;
+  -- By the well-foundedness of $R$, we can apply induction on the height of $v$.
+  have h_ind : ∀ h : ℕ, ∀ v : F.World, F.R w v → (Nat.card {u : F.World | F.R v u}) = h → v ∈ S := by
+    intros h v hv hv_card
+    induction' h using Nat.strong_induction_on with h ih generalizing v;
+    have hv'_card : ∀ u : F.World, F.R v u → Nat.card { u' : F.World | F.R u u' } < h := by
+      intros u hu
+      have hu_subset : {u' : F.World | F.R u u'} ⊂ {u' : F.World | F.R v u'} := by
+        simp_all +decide [ Set.ssubset_def, Set.subset_def ];
+        exact ⟨ fun x hx => F.trans _ _ _ hu hx, u, hu, F.irrefl _ ⟩;
+      convert Set.ncard_lt_ncard hu_subset using 1;
+      exact hv_card.symm;
+    have hv'_in_S : ∀ u : F.World, F.R v u → u ∈ S := by
+      grind +suggestions;
+    grind +locals;
+  exact h_ind _ _ hv rfl
+
+/-! ## Part 4: Upward-Closed Sets Form a Provability Lattice -/
+
+/-- A set is **upward closed** in a GL frame if it is closed under the
+    accessibility relation. -/
+def GLFrame.IsUpwardClosed (F : GLFrame) (S : Set F.World) : Prop :=
+  ∀ w ∈ S, ∀ v, F.R w v → v ∈ S
+
+/-
+The set of upward-closed subsets is closed under intersection.
+-/
+theorem upward_closed_inter (F : GLFrame) (S T : Set F.World)
+    (hS : F.IsUpwardClosed S) (hT : F.IsUpwardClosed T) :
+    F.IsUpwardClosed (S ∩ T) := by
+  exact fun w hw v hv => ⟨ hS w hw.1 v hv, hT w hw.2 v hv ⟩
+
+/-
+The set of upward-closed subsets is closed under union.
+-/
+theorem upward_closed_union (F : GLFrame) (S T : Set F.World)
+    (hS : F.IsUpwardClosed S) (hT : F.IsUpwardClosed T) :
+    F.IsUpwardClosed (S ∪ T) := by
+  intro w hw v hv; cases hw <;> aesop;
+
+/-
+univ is upward closed.
+-/
+theorem upward_closed_univ (F : GLFrame) : F.IsUpwardClosed (Set.univ : Set F.World) := by
+  exact fun _ _ _ _ => trivial
+
+/-
+∅ is upward closed.
+-/
+theorem upward_closed_empty (F : GLFrame) : F.IsUpwardClosed (∅ : Set F.World) := by
+  -- The empty set is upward closed because there are no elements to check.
+  simp [GLFrame.IsUpwardClosed]
+
+/-
+□S is always upward closed (by transitivity of R).
+-/
+theorem box_upward_closed (F : GLFrame) (S : Set F.World) :
+    F.IsUpwardClosed (F.boxSet S) := by
+  intro w hw v hv; exact fun u hu => hw u ( F.trans _ _ _ hv hu ) ;
+
+/-! ## Part 5: Well-Foundedness of GL Frames -/
+
+/-
+In a finite transitive irreflexive frame, the accessibility relation
+    is well-founded. This is the key structural property that makes GL
+    work: it ensures that inductive arguments over accessibility terminate.
+-/
+theorem gl_frame_well_founded (F : GLFrame) : WellFounded F.R := by
+  have h_wf : ∀ (s : Finset F.World), s.Nonempty → ∃ w ∈ s, ∀ v ∈ s, ¬F.R v w := by
+    intro s hs; induction' s using Finset.induction_on with w s ih; aesop;
+    by_cases hs : s.Nonempty <;> simp_all +decide [ Finset.Nonempty ];
+    · grind +suggestions;
+    · exact F.irrefl w;
+    · exact Classical.decEq _;

+
+/-! ## Part 6: Maximal Worlds and Completeness -/
+
+/-- A world is **maximal** (a dead end) if it has no accessible successors.
+    Maximal worlds correspond to complete consistent theories. -/
+def GLFrame.IsMaximal (F : GLFrame) (w : F.World) : Prop :=
+  ∀ v, ¬ F.R w v
+
+/-
+At a maximal world, □S is automatically satisfied for any S
+    (vacuous truth).
+-/
+theorem box_at_maximal (F : GLFrame) (w : F.World) (S : Set F.World)
+    (hmax : F.IsMaximal w) : w ∈ F.boxSet S := by
+  exact fun v hv => False.elim ( hmax v hv )

+/-

+    This follows from well-foundedness: any minimal element under
+    the reverse of R is maximal.

+theorem box_diamond_dual (F : GLFrame) (S : Set F.World) :

+
+/-- The **theory space** construction: given a provability lattice L,
+    we can construct a "frame of filters" where worlds are proper filters
+    (representing consistent complete theories) and accessibility
+    is reverse inclusion (stronger theories see weaker ones).

+    This is a categorical dual to the Lindenbaum construction. -/
+structure TheoryWorld (L : ProvabilityLattice) where
+  /-- The filter (consistent theory) -/
+  filter : Set L.carrier
+  /-- Upward closed -/
+  up_closed : ∀ a ∈ filter, ∀ b, a ≤ b → b ∈ filter
+  /-- Closed under meets -/
+  meet_closed : ∀ a ∈ filter, ∀ b ∈ filter, a ⊓ b ∈ filter
+  /-- Proper: ⊥ ∉ filter (consistency) -/
+  proper : ⊥ ∉ filter
+  /-- Contains ⊤ -/
+  has_top : ⊤ ∈ filter
+
+/-- Two theory worlds are related if the first extends the second
+    (the first is a stronger theory). -/
+def TheoryWorld.extends_ {L : ProvabilityLattice} (w v : TheoryWorld L) : Prop :=
+  v.filter ⊂ w.filter
+
+/-
+The extension relation is irreflexive (no theory strictly extends itself).
+-/
+theorem theory_extends_irrefl {L : ProvabilityLattice} (w : TheoryWorld L) :
+    ¬ w.extends_ w := by
+  unfold TheoryWorld.extends_;
+  simp +decide [ Set.ssubset_def ]
+
+/-
+The extension relation is transitive.
+-/
+theorem theory_extends_trans {L : ProvabilityLattice}
+    (w v u : TheoryWorld L) :
+    w.extends_ v → v.extends_ u → w.extends_ u := by
+  exact fun h1 h2 => h2.trans h1

/-!
# Hydrogen Atom: The Energy Spectrum

The bound-state energy levels of the hydrogen atom are the Bohr levels
`E_n = -1/n²` for `n ∈ ℕ₊`, and the continuous (scattering) spectrum is
`[0, ∞)`. This file formalizes the *set* of spectral values

  `S = {-1/n² : n ∈ ℕ₊} ∪ [0, ∞)`

and proves its structural properties: the discrete levels are strictly
negative and strictly increasing, they accumulate only at `0`, the whole
set `S` is closed, and the degeneracy of level `n` equals `n²`.

## Main results
* `bohrEnergy_neg`, `bohrEnergy_strictMono` — sign and monotonicity.
* `bohrEnergy_tendsto_zero` — the discrete levels accumulate at `0`.
* `bohrEnergy_ge_neg_one` — the ground state `-1` is the minimum.
* `hydrogenSpectrum_isClosed` — `S` is closed.
* `discrete_disjoint_continuous` — bound and scattering parts are disjoint.
* `hydrogen_degeneracy` — `∑_{l<n} (2l+1) = n²`.
* `rydberg_emission_pos` — emission frequency `E_n - E_m > 0` for `m < n`.

-- !-- Lab Notes -- !--
Hypothesis: the hydrogen point spectrum `{-1/n²}` together with the
continuum `[0,∞)` forms a *closed* subset of ℝ, with the discrete part
accumulating exactly at the bottom of the continuum.
Experiment: define `bohrEnergy`, prove sign/monotonicity/limit, then show
closedness by exhibiting `S` as `(range bohrEnergy) ∪ Ici 0` whose only
discrete limit point `0` lies in `Ici 0`.
Analysis: the n²-degeneracy `∑_{l<n}(2l+1)=n²` is the arithmetic backbone of
the accidental SO(4) symmetry; it survived immediately by induction.
Closedness was the hard step — it needs the limit `bohrEnergy n → 0`.
Critique: `bohrEnergy` is genuinely negative (not vacuous); closedness uses a
real topological argument, not `decide`.
Synthesis: a self-contained description of the hydrogen spectrum as a set.
-- !-- end Lab Notes -- !--
-/

open Filter Topology Set
open scoped BigOperators

/-- The Bohr energy level `E_n = -1/n²` (in Rydberg units). -/
def bohrEnergy (n : ℕ+) : ℝ := -1 / ((n : ℝ) ^ 2)

/-
Every Bohr level is strictly negative.
-/
theorem bohrEnergy_neg (n : ℕ+) : bohrEnergy n < 0 := by
  exact div_neg_of_neg_of_pos ( by norm_num ) ( by positivity )

/-
The ground state `E_1 = -1` is a lower bound for all levels.
-/
theorem bohrEnergy_ge_neg_one (n : ℕ+) : (-1 : ℝ) ≤ bohrEnergy n := by
  exact le_trans ( by norm_num ) ( mul_le_mul_of_nonpos_left ( inv_anti₀ ( by positivity ) ( pow_le_pow_left₀ ( by positivity ) ( Nat.one_le_cast.2 n.2 ) 2 ) ) ( by norm_num ) )

/-
`E_1 = -1`.
-/
theorem bohrEnergy_one : bohrEnergy 1 = -1 := by
  unfold bohrEnergy; norm_num

/-
The Bohr levels are strictly increasing in `n` (they rise towards `0`).
-/
theorem bohrEnergy_strictMono : StrictMono bohrEnergy := by
  intro m n hmn;
  unfold bohrEnergy; rw [ div_lt_div_iff₀ ] <;> norm_num ; nlinarith [ show ( m : ℝ ) ≥ 1 from Nat.one_le_cast.mpr m.pos, show ( n : ℝ ) ≥ m + 1 from mod_cast hmn ] ;

/-
The discrete levels accumulate at `0`.
-/
theorem bohrEnergy_tendsto_zero :
    Tendsto (fun n : ℕ+ => bohrEnergy n) atTop (𝓝 0) := by
  refine' squeeze_zero_norm' _ _;
  exacts [ fun n => 1 / ( n : ℝ ) ^ 2, Filter.Eventually.of_forall fun n => by unfold bohrEnergy; norm_num [ abs_div ], tendsto_const_nhds.div_atTop <| Filter.Tendsto.comp ( Filter.tendsto_pow_atTop ( by norm_num ) ) <| tendsto_natCast_atTop_atTop.comp <| Filter.tendsto_atTop_atTop.2 fun x => ⟨ ⟨ x + 1, Nat.succ_pos x ⟩, fun n hn => Nat.le_of_succ_le hn ⟩ ]

/-- The full hydrogen spectrum: discrete Bohr levels together with the
continuum `[0, ∞)`. -/
def hydrogenSpectrum : Set ℝ :=
  (Set.range bohrEnergy) ∪ Set.Ici 0

/-
The discrete (bound) and continuous (scattering) parts are disjoint.
-/
theorem discrete_disjoint_continuous :
    Disjoint (Set.range bohrEnergy) (Set.Ici (0 : ℝ)) := by
  norm_num [ Set.disjoint_left ];
  exact fun a => bohrEnergy_neg a

The hydrogen spectrum is a closed subset of ℝ.
-/
theorem hydrogenSpectrum_isClosed : IsClosed hydrogenSpectrum := by
  unfold hydrogenSpectrum;
  -- The range of a sequence together with its limit is closed.
  have h_closed : IsClosed (Set.range bohrEnergy ∪ {0}) := by
    refine' IsCompact.isClosed ( _ );
    have h_compact : Filter.Tendsto (fun n : ℕ+ => bohrEnergy n) Filter.atTop (nhds 0) := by
      convert bohrEnergy_tendsto_zero using 1;
    have h_compact : IsCompact (insert 0 (Set.range (fun n : ℕ => bohrEnergy (⟨n + 1, Nat.succ_pos n⟩)))) := by

    ext; simp [Set.mem_insert_iff];
    exact or_congr Iff.rfl ⟨ fun ⟨ y, hy ⟩ => ⟨ y - 1, by cases y using PNat.recOn <;> tauto ⟩, fun ⟨ y, hy ⟩ => ⟨ ⟨ y + 1, Nat.succ_pos y ⟩, hy ⟩ ⟩;

The degeneracy of energy level `n` is `n²`: summing `2l+1` over the
orbital quantum numbers `l = 0, …, n-1`.

theorem hydrogen_degeneracy (n : ℕ) :
    ∑ l ∈ Finset.range n, (2 * l + 1) = n ^ 2 := by
  induction n with
  | zero => simp
  | succ k ih => rw [Finset.sum_range_succ, ih]; ring

Emission line frequency `E_n - E_m` is positive for `m < n`

theorem rydberg_emission_pos (m n : ℕ+) (h : m < n) :

import Mathlib

/-!
# Krawtchouk Polynomials for Quantum Coding Theory

Krawtchouk polynomials K_j(x; n) are the fundamental discrete orthogonal
polynomials appearing in coding theory. They form the character table of the
binary Hamming association scheme H(n, 2) and are the kernel of the
MacWilliams transform relating a code's weight enumerator to its dual.

## Main Definitions

* `krawtchouk` — K_j(x; n) = Σ_{l=0}^{j} (-1)^l · C(x,l) · C(n-x, j-l)
* `krawtchoukReal` — real-valued version for weight enumerator analysis

## Main Results

* `krawtchouk_zero_index` — K_0(x; n) = 1
* `krawtchouk_at_zero` — K_j(0; n) = C(n, j)
* `krawtchouk_one` — K_1(x; n) = n - 2x
* `krawtchouk_at_n` — K_j(n; n) = (-1)^j · C(n, j)
* `krawtchouk_eigenvalue_hamming` — eigenvalue interpretation

## References

* MacWilliams, F.J. and Sloane, N.J.A. "The Theory of Error-Correcting Codes"
* Shor, P.W. and Laflamme, R. "Quantum Analog of the MacWilliams Identities"
-/

open Finset BigOperators Nat

/-! ## Section 1: Definition -/

/-- The Krawtchouk polynomial K_j(x; n) for binary codes of length n.
    K_j(x; n) = Σ_{l=0}^{j} (-1)^l · C(x, l) · C(n-x, j-l)

    This is the standard form from MacWilliams-Sloane. The polynomial gives
    the eigenvalue of the j-th distance matrix of the Hamming scheme on the
    eigenspace indexed by x. -/
def krawtchouk (n j x : ℕ) : ℤ :=
  ∑ l ∈ Finset.range (j + 1),
    (-1 : ℤ) ^ l * (x.choose l : ℤ) * ((n - x).choose (j - l) : ℤ)

/-- Real-valued Krawtchouk polynomial. -/
noncomputable def krawtchoukReal (n j x : ℕ) : ℝ := (krawtchouk n j x : ℝ)

/-! ## Section 2: Basic Evaluations -/

/-- **K_0(x; n) = 1**: The zeroth Krawtchouk polynomial is identically 1.
    This is because the sum has a single term with l=0. -/
theorem krawtchouk_zero_index (n x : ℕ) : krawtchouk n 0 x = 1 := by
  simp [krawtchouk]

/-
**K_j(0; n) = C(n, j)**: Evaluating at x=0 gives the binomial coefficient.
    When x=0, C(0, l) = 0 for l ≥ 1, so only the l=0 term survives.
-/
theorem krawtchouk_at_zero (n j : ℕ) : krawtchouk n j 0 = (n.choose j : ℤ) := by
  unfold krawtchouk;
  rw [ Finset.sum_range_succ' ] ; aesop

/-
**K_1(x; n) = n - 2x**: The first Krawtchouk polynomial is linear.
    Proof: K_1(x;n) = C(n-x, 1) - C(x, 1) · C(n-x, 0) = (n-x) - x = n - 2x.
-/
theorem krawtchouk_one (n x : ℕ) (hx : x ≤ n) :
    krawtchouk n 1 x = (n : ℤ) - 2 * (x : ℤ) := by
  unfold krawtchouk;
  norm_num [ Finset.sum_range_succ ] ; linarith [ Nat.sub_add_cancel hx ]

/-
**K_j(n; n) = (-1)^j · C(n, j)**: Evaluation at x = n.
    When x = n, C(n-n, j-l) = C(0, j-l) = δ_{l,j}, so only l = j survives.
-/
theorem krawtchouk_at_n (n j : ℕ) (hj : j ≤ n) :
    krawtchouk n j n = (-1 : ℤ) ^ j * (n.choose j : ℤ) := by
  unfold krawtchouk;
  simp +decide [ Finset.sum_range_succ, Nat.choose_eq_zero_of_lt ];
  exact Finset.sum_eq_zero fun x hx => by rw [ Nat.choose_eq_zero_of_lt ( Nat.sub_pos_of_lt ( Finset.mem_range.mp hx ) ) ] ; ring;

/-! ## Section 3: Algebraic Properties -/

/-
The Krawtchouk polynomial K_j(x; n) for j > n is zero.
    This is because C(n-x, j-l) = 0 when j - l > n - x for all valid l.
-/
theorem krawtchouk_eq_zero_of_gt (n j x : ℕ) (hj : n < j) (hx : x ≤ n) :
    krawtchouk n j x = 0 := by
  have h_zero : ∀ l, l ≤ j → (-1 : ℤ)^l * (x.choose l : ℤ) * ((n - x).choose (j - l) : ℤ) = 0 := by
    intro l hl; by_cases hl' : l ≤ x <;> simp_all +decide [ Nat.choose_eq_zero_of_lt ] ;
    exact Or.inr ( Nat.choose_eq_zero_of_lt ( by omega ) );
  exact Finset.sum_eq_zero fun l hl => h_zero l <| Finset.mem_range_succ_iff.mp hl

/-- The eigenvalue connection: K_1(j; n) = n - 2j.
    The first-distance matrix of H(n,2) has eigenvalue n - 2j on eigenspace j.
    This connects quantum weight analysis to spectral graph theory. -/
theorem krawtchouk_eigenvalue_hamming (n j : ℕ) (hj : j ≤ n) :
    krawtchouk n 1 j = (n : ℤ) - 2 * (j : ℤ) :=
  krawtchouk_one n j hj

/-! ## Section 4: Computational Verification

These verify our definition against known values. While proved by `native_decide`,

/-- K_2(1; 5) = C(4,2) - C(1,1)·C(4,1) + C(1,2)·C(4,0) = 6 - 4 + 0 = 2 -/
example : krawtchouk 5 2 1 = 2 := by native_decide

/-- K_3(1; 7) = C(6,3) - C(1,1)·C(6,2) + C(1,2)·C(6,1) - C(1,3)·C(6,0)

/-- Verification: K_1(0; 5) = 5 = C(5,1) -/
example : krawtchouk 5 1 0 = 5 := by native_decide

/-- Verification: K_1(3; 7) = 7 - 6 = 1 -/
example : krawtchouk 7 1 3 = 1 := by native_decide

  discrete part, namely 0, already lies in [0, ∞).

## 2. Degeneracy of level n

Energy E_n depends only on the principal quantum number n; for fixed n the
orbital quantum number ranges l = 0,…,n-1 and each l carries 2l+1 magnetic
substates. Total degeneracy (ignoring spin):

  g(n) = Σ_{l=0}^{n-1} (2l+1)

| n | g(n) | n² |
|---|------|----|
| 1 | 1 | 1 |
| 2 | 4 | 4 |
| 3 | 9 | 9 |
| 4 | 16 | 16 |

So g(n) = n² exactly (OEIS A000290, the squares). This is the classic
n²-fold degeneracy of the hydrogen atom.

## 3. Rydberg transition frequencies E_n - E_m (m < n)

Emission n → m releases ΔE = E_n - E_m = 1/m² - 1/n² > 0.

Lyman (m=1): 1 - 1/4 = 0.7500, 1 - 1/9 = 0.8889, …
Balmer (m=2): 1/4 - 1/9 = 0.1389, 1/4 - 1/16 = 0.1875, …

All positive for n > m, confirming emission lines.

## 4. Selection rules

Electric-dipole operator has odd parity; spherical harmonic Y_l^m has parity
(-1)^l. A matrix element ⟨l'|r|l⟩ is nonzero only if l + l' is odd (parity) and
|l - l'| ≤ 1 (triangle / Wigner-Eckart, dipole is rank-1). The only integers l'
satisfying both |l - l'| ≤ 1 and l + l' odd are l' = l ± 1, giving Δl = ±1.
For the magnetic number the azimuthal integral ∫₀²π e^{i(m'-m-q)φ}dφ forces
m' - m = q ∈ {-1,0,1}, i.e. Δm ∈ {-1,0,1}.

## 5. Azimuthal eigenfunctions

L_z = -i ∂/∂φ acting on e^{imφ} gives -i·(im)·e^{imφ} = m·e^{imφ}, so e^{imφ}
is an L_z-eigenfunction with eigenvalue m (verified analytically; formalized via
`HasDerivAt`).

# Future Directions — Spectral Theory of Hydrogen

Derived from the Stage 3/4 findings of this research cycle (files
`Physics/HydrogenSpectrum.lean` and the extended `Physics/AngularMomentum.lean`).

## What this cycle established (anchor results)
- `bohrEnergy n = -1/n²` is strictly increasing, bounded below by `-1`, and
  `→ 0`; hence the point spectrum accumulates only at `0`.
- `hydrogenSpectrum = range bohrEnergy ∪ [0,∞)` is **closed** in ℝ, and the
  bound/scattering parts are **disjoint**.
- Degeneracy `∑_{l<n}(2l+1) = n²`.
- `e^{imφ}` is an exact `L_z = -i∂φ` eigenfunction with eigenvalue `m`
  (`Lz_azimuthal_eigen`), unit modulus.
- Orbital selection rule as a sharp `iff` (`dipole_selection_l`) and magnetic
  selection rule from azimuthal orthogonality (`magnetic_selection`).

## Conjectures

### 1. The discrete hydrogen spectrum is exactly the accumulation-point closure of a geometric-like sequence
Claim: `closure (range bohrEnergy) = range bohrEnergy ∪ {0}`, and `0` is the
unique accumulation point; moreover `range bohrEnergy` is order-isomorphic to
ℕ⁺ with the reverse order.
The key insight is that `-1/n²` is strictly monotone with a single limit, so its
range is a discrete set whose only frontier point is the infimum of the
continuum — the topological signature separating bound states from scattering.
Why now? `hydrogenSpectrum_isClosed` already isolates `0` as the lone limit via
`Filter.Tendsto.isCompact_insert_range`; upgrading "closed" to an explicit
closure description is a short next step on the same machinery.

### 2. n²-degeneracy is forced by SO(4), not SO(3)
Claim: the multiplicity `n² = ∑_{l<n}(2l+1)` equals `dim` of an irreducible
representation of `SO(4)` (specifically `(n-1)/2 ⊗ (n-1)/2`), so the "accidental"
degeneracy is the dimension `((n-1)+1)² = n²` of a `Spin(4)=SU(2)×SU(2)` rep.
The key insight is that `∑_{l<n}(2l+1)` telescopes to a perfect square exactly
because two copies of spin-`(n-1)/2` (each of dimension `n`) tensor to `n²`.
Why now? The arithmetic identity is already formalized (`hydrogen_degeneracy`);
pairing it with the existing `l=1` `so(3)` matrix algebra in
`AngularMomentum.lean` gives a concrete first `SU(2)×SU(2)` instance to verify.

### 3. The selection rules are exactly the support of a rank-1 tensor product
Claim: `dipoleAllowedL l l'` holds iff the trivial representation appears in
`(spin l) ⊗ (spin 1) ⊗ (spin l')` AND the parities multiply to `-1`; equivalently
the nonzero dipole channels are the lattice points of the `(l,1,l')` triangle
intersected with the odd-parity sublattice.
The key insight is that both mechanisms we proved separately — triangle
(`|l-l'|≤1`) and parity (`Odd (l+l')`) — are the two defining constraints of a
Clebsch–Gordan/Wigner-3j nonvanishing condition for a rank-1 operator.
Why now? `dipole_selection_l` already proves the `iff` at the integer level;
recasting `|l-l'|≤1` as a Clebsch–Gordan triangle is the natural bridge to a
general Wigner-Eckart statement.

### 4. Rydberg frequencies are dense modulo the continuum edge
Claim: the set of emission frequencies `{1/m² - 1/n² : 1 ≤ m < n}` has `0` and
every `1/m²` as accumulation points, and its closure is
`{1/m² : m ≥ 1} ∪ {0}` translated — a self-similar (fractal-like) frequency comb.
The key insight is that fixing the lower level `m` and letting `n→∞` makes each
spectral series (Lyman, Balmer, …) converge to its series limit `1/m²`, and
these limits themselves accumulate at `0`.
Why now? `rydberg_emission_pos` and `bohrEnergy_tendsto_zero` already give
positivity and the `n→∞` limit; assembling the two-parameter accumulation
structure reuses exactly these lemmas.

### 5. Unit-modulus azimuthal modes give an exact orthonormal L_z-eigenbasis
Claim: `{ (2π)^{-1/2} e^{imφ} : m ∈ ℤ }` is a Hilbert basis of `L²(S¹)`
consisting of `L_z`-eigenfunctions, and the dipole matrix element
`⟨m'|e^{iqφ}|m⟩` is `2π·δ_{m',m+q}` — i.e. the selection rule is literally a
basis-orthogonality statement.
The key insight is that `azimuthalExp_norm` (unit modulus) plus
`azimuthal_orthogonality` already supply normalization and orthogonality, the
two axioms of an orthonormal eigenbasis.
Why now? `azimuthal_dipole_integral` proves the `2π·δ` matrix element verbatim;
promoting the family to a `HilbertBasis`/`OrthonormalBasis` in Mathlib is the
remaining functional-analytic step.
